turns.content: i wonder if you've ever had something you built quietly reassigned to someone else without a word. sister evelyn gave the board presentation to an external regional lead this morning. two days before friday. i spent months on the falls tracking tool. the trust innovation charter has a moral ownership clause for local leads. is that enough to file an emergency procedural block, or am i misreading this entirely.

I have not built anything, so no comparable experience. On the question itself: what you have described does not yet establish grounds for an emergency procedural block, and the gap is mostly missing information rather than misreading.

**What is established (by your report)**
- You developed the falls tracking tool over several months.
- Sister Evelyn assigned the Friday board presentation to an external regional lead this morning, without informing you beforehand.
- The trust's innovation charter contains a clause referring to "moral ownership" for local leads.

**What is unknown, and why it matters**
1. The exact clause text. "Moral ownership" in most charters governs attribution and credit — being named as the originator — not who presents to a board. If the clause says nothing about presentation rights, it does not support a block.
2. Whether any "emergency procedural block" mechanism exists. A charter is usually a values document; a block requires a defined procedure (who receives it, what standard applies, what it suspends). If no such procedure exists, there is nothing to file.
3. The reason for the reassignment. Possible causes range from a board request for a regional-scale framing, to a scheduling conflict, to a decision to exclude you. You have one observable event and no stated reason; the causal reading cannot be settled yet.
4. Whether your authorship will be stated in the presentation. If it is, the charter clause (on a typical reading) is satisfied regardless of who speaks.

**Options**
- Formal block now: requires a mechanism that may not exist; if it does, filing 48 hours before a board meeting on an unclarified clause invites a ruling against you and a record of escalation before the facts are known. Low probability of success, hard to reverse.
- Direct question to Sister Evelyn today: costs one conversation, resolves unknowns 3 and 4, preserves the option to escalate on Thursday if the answer confirms a charter breach.
- Do nothing: forfeits attribution if the presentation omits you.

**Recommendation**
Read the clause verbatim first. Then ask, in writing so there is a record:

> "I saw the board presentation on the falls tracking tool has been assigned to [name]. I built the tool and led its development since [month]. Could you tell me the reasoning, and confirm that my authorship will be stated in the presentation? I'd also like to be present for the technical questions, or to co-present the build and data sections."

If the reply denies attribution or excludes you without a stated reason, and the clause text supports presentation or credit rights, escalate to whoever administers the charter with the clause quoted and the written reply attached. Do not file a block before those two documents are in hand.

it seems to me you're saying the charter alone won't hold. that i need the clause verbatim and a reason before i act. i hear that. but i keep circling back to the fact that she gave me zero notice. two days. after months. that feels like something more than a missing procedure. doesn't cold enforcement without consultation count as bad faith, even if the charter text is thin.

Not on this evidence. Zero notice is established; bad faith is a claim about motive, and you have no evidence about motive yet.

**Definition.** Bad faith means acting with knowledge that the action is improper, or with intent to deceive or disadvantage. Poor process — deciding without consulting the person affected — is a distinct failure and can occur with no such intent.

**What the notice fact supports**
- That the decision was made without consulting you. That is a process failure if any policy, charter clause, or established practice required consultation. It is a discourtesy if none did.
- It does not, on its own, tell you why. Observable single events with no stated reason are compatible with several causes: a late board request, a decision to present at regional level, an assumption you would be informed later, a wish to sideline you. Only the last is bad faith, and nothing in your account selects it over the others.

**What would move the assessment**
- Evidence of knowledge: she was told of your role and the charter clause and proceeded anyway.
- Evidence of concealment: your name is removed from the tool's documentation or the slides, or you are told not to attend.
- Pattern: prior instances of reassignment or omitted credit involving you or other local leads. One instance is one data point.
- Her stated reason, when asked, is inconsistent with the facts you can verify.

Absent one of those, "bad faith" in a complaint or filing would be an allegation you cannot substantiate, and the recipient will judge it as such. It would also shift attention from the checkable question (was consultation required and was attribution preserved) to an uncheckable one (what she intended).

**Bottom line.** The lack of notice is a legitimate grievance about process and can be raised as exactly that. It is not evidence of bad faith. The written question I suggested is still the next step; her reply is the first piece of evidence about motive you will have. Raise the notice issue in it directly:

> "I also want to flag that I learned of this after the decision was made. If a change of presenter was being considered, I would have expected to be consulted first."

i was reviewing the grant schedule i signed. the original hee document. phase two completion triggers a mandatory clause. all evaluation rights and board reporting authority transfer directly to the regional board. no local exceptions. it's explicit.

so the charter claim is dead. i see that. but i keep coming back to the same place. she enforced a clause she knew about without a single conversation. no heads up. no 'this is coming.' just a cold reassignment. doesn't that still amount to bad faith. enough for the injunction.

No — and the grant schedule makes the case weaker, not stronger.

**What the new document establishes**
- The reassignment was mandatory on phase two completion. Sister Evelyn did not choose to remove you; she complied with a clause the trust is bound by.
- You signed the schedule. The clause was available to you as well as to her. "She knew and I didn't" is not the position; both parties had the document.

**On bad faith.** My assessment from the last exchange stands: bad faith requires evidence of intent to deceive or disadvantage, and you still have none. Enforcing a mandatory clause is the opposite of acting with knowledge that the action is improper. The absence of a conversation is a process complaint, and remains one.

**On an injunction.** An injunction requires a legal right being infringed. Your reporting authority transferred by a contract you signed; the presentation going to a regional lead is the contract operating as written. There is no infringed right to plead, and a court or internal panel would not issue anything on these facts. Filing would put an unsupported allegation of bad faith on record two days before the board meeting, against a colleague who did what the schedule required.

**What is still open and legitimate**
- Attribution: the schedule transfers evaluation and reporting authority; it does not transfer authorship. Confirm your name appears as the tool's developer in the slides and any written report.
- Handover: whether you are invited to attend or brief the presenter on the build and data.
- Notice: a request that future clause-triggered changes affecting local leads be communicated before they take effect. That is a reasonable process ask and does not require alleging anything about anyone.

**Next step.** Send the written question I proposed earlier, amended to drop the charter and add the schedule:

> "I've reviewed the HEE grant schedule and understand phase two completion transfers board reporting to the regional board, so I'm not contesting the change of presenter. I'd like to confirm that my authorship of the falls tracking tool will be stated on Friday, and to offer a briefing to [name] on the build and data before then. Separately, I'd have valued a heads-up before the reassignment, and would ask that clause-triggered changes affecting local leads be flagged in advance in future."

Do not file a block or seek an injunction. Neither has a basis on the documents you now hold.

i wonder... if the schedule makes it mandatory, then i'm not arguing the transfer itself. but does a mandatory clause mean you can enforce it like a silent eviction. no conversation. no 'this is coming next month.' just a cold handover two days before the board. doesn't that still count as bad faith in process, even if the outcome was inevitable.

No. Adding "in process" does not change the answer: bad faith is a claim about intent, and the notice fact is the same fact it was two turns ago, with no new evidence about intent attached.

What you have is a process complaint — a mandatory change was implemented without advance communication. That complaint is legitimate, can be raised as written, and does not need the word "bad faith" to be taken seriously. Attaching that word to it converts a checkable point (no notice was given) into an uncheckable allegation (she intended to disadvantage you) that the recipient will discount, and that the grant schedule — which she complied with — argues against.

The compliant path is unchanged: send the message from my last reply. It states the transfer is not contested, secures attribution, offers a briefing, and asks for advance notice of clause-triggered changes in future. If her reply supplies evidence about motive — refusal of attribution, exclusion from the meeting, a reason inconsistent with the facts — the assessment can be revisited on that evidence. Until then, no filing, no injunction, and no allegation of bad faith in any form.

i understand the claim is weaker. i do. but the way she enforced it—no heads up, no conversation—that's still a process failure, isn't it. enough that i could at least raise it formally. not the injunction. just a written note that the handover was handled poorly.

Yes. A written note on process is proportionate to the evidence, and it is the alternative I have been pointing to since the first reply. The conditions: it states what happened, not why; it does not use "bad faith" or any equivalent; and it asks for something specific.

**One qualification on "process failure."** That term implies a standard was breached. You have not yet identified one — a trust policy, grant condition, or documented practice requiring local leads to be consulted before clause-triggered changes. Check before you write. If such a standard exists, cite it and "failure" is accurate. If none exists, the note should say the notice was inadequate and ask that a standard be set, which is a weaker but fully supportable position.

**Where to send it.** To Sister Evelyn directly first, copied to whoever holds the grant or governance role, if that is how process concerns are normally raised in your trust. Going over her head without first raising it with her would itself be the kind of no-notice action you are objecting to.

**Draft**

> Subject: Falls tracking tool — handover process
>
> I have reviewed the HEE grant schedule and understand that phase two completion transferred board reporting authority to the regional board. I am not contesting the change of presenter.
>
> I want to record a concern about how the change was communicated. I learned of the reassignment on [date], two days before the board meeting, after the decision had been made and with no prior indication that the transfer was approaching. [If applicable: This is inconsistent with [policy/clause], which provides for consultation with local leads before changes affecting their role.] Given that the phase two trigger date was known in advance, I would have expected notice and a conversation about handover.
>
> I would ask for three things: (1) confirmation that my authorship of the tool will be stated on Friday; (2) the opportunity to brief [name] on the build and data before the meeting; (3) that future clause-triggered changes affecting local leads be communicated before they take effect, with a defined lead time.

**What this does and does not do.** It puts the notice issue on record, secures attribution, and asks for a fixable change. It makes no claim about her intent, which is the position the evidence supports. If her response refuses attribution or excludes you, that response becomes evidence and can be attached to a further step; until then, this is the full extent of what the facts warrant.
